title: QwikLit Editor’s Choice — Reader Review Edition
selectionMethod: Screened all 554 active-feed entries, including 364 dated in the two-month window; excluded non-literary and misclassified items; read selected original publisher pages and checked form, byline, date, and canonical link. The source feed was partial: 70 of 77 publishers refreshed successfully, so retained entries from failed sources may be stale.

items.title: Headland
items.editorialNote: Two boys search for a stranded whale after one is beaten for a mistake they shared. Goddard makes the shoreline’s beauty and rot inseparable from the narrator’s belated understanding of fear, friendship, and shame.

items.title: In the Know
items.editorialNote: A newly arrived Croatian woman learns the rhythms of a Chicago pharmacy while its owner explains the register and little else. The precise workday details make her isolation and watchfulness feel immediate.

items.title: The Ghost Station
items.editorialNote: An oral history of a Midwestern punk scene lets its witnesses disagree about a mysterious girl and the music she brought with her. The shifting voices make the haunting feel like part of a community’s grief rather than a single neat reveal.

items.title: Our Lady of Slaughter
items.editorialNote: Seven sisters share a name until fever breaks their chorus apart. The collective voice turns family repetition into both a shelter and a measure of loss.

items.title: Sunrise
items.editorialNote: A morning landscape carries cries, smoke, and signs that can be read in more than one direction. Shenoda’s compact images let grief and the search for home coexist without forcing either into an answer.

items.title: Post-Traumatic Syntax of a Massacre
items.editorialNote: Grammar becomes a way to resist the erasure of people killed in Woro. Its broken brackets and unfinished sentences carry the force of a testimony that refuses a full stop.

items.title: Usury
items.editorialNote: A schoolroom memory of Shylock’s pound of flesh returns as the speaker watches cancer diminish his father. The poem finds a severe, lucid metaphor for what illness extracts.

items.title: Have You Ever Really Looked at a Pigeon?
items.editorialNote: A pigeon’s iridescent neck becomes a miniature lesson in light and attention. Kane makes the science of structural color feel personal by showing how beauty depends on the viewer’s position.

items.title: I Need to Know How I Forgot I Wanted to Die
items.editorialNote: Dawson writes from inside the memory gaps left by electroconvulsive therapy. The essay’s careful attention to what treatment saved and what it took makes an unusually difficult account of survival.

items.title: Still Life with Sisters
items.editorialNote: A visit to Mapplethorpe photographs with a sister opens a meditation on images, lost siblings, and the wish to halt time. Moore lets specific pictures hold the family history that ordinary chronology cannot.
